A comatose male patient of middle age is brought to the emergency department with active rectal
bleeding. He has no known medical history. His vital signs show: pulse 119/min, blood pressure 127/69
mm Hg, respiratory rate 22/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. His extremities are cold.
Laboratory results reveal: hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL, hematocrit 30%, BUN 33 mg/dL, and normal PT/aPTT.
After initial resuscitation with IV fluids and blood transfusion, his vital signs stabilize. A nasogastric tube
insertion shows bile-stained fluid without blood. Rectal examination and proctoscopy demonstrate
significant active bleeding at an estimated rate of 2-3 mL/min, with no evident hemorrhoids or fissures.
What should be the next diagnostic step? Answer Choices: (A) Repeat nasogastric lavage (B)
Exploratory laparotomy with segmental bowel resection (C) Colonoscopy (D) Push enteroscopy (E)
Capsule endoscopy (F) Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) (G) CT angiography of the abdomen
and pelvis (H) Mesenteric angiography (I) Upper endoscopy (J) Tagged red blood cell scintigraphy
 A. Exploratory laparotomy with segmental bowel resection
B. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA)
C. Mesenteric angiography
D. CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis
E. Push enteroscopy
F. Repeat nasogastric lavage
G. Tagged red blood cell scintigraphy
H. Capsule endoscopy
I. Colonoscopy
J. Upper endoscopy
